extracted.intended_audience: individual internet subscribers and consumer advocates encouraged to file comments with the FCC
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for individuals on submitting effective public comments to the FCC about broadband service problems; emphasizes concrete, dated, provider-named incidents that demonstrate consumer harm and support rulemaking. Aimed at building an evidentiary record to influence broadband policy, funding, and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: State whether you have been adequately served by your ISP
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should address whether you have "been adequately served by your internet service provider (ISP)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core question FCC is asking — explicitly answer if your service met expectations or not, and in what ways it failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specific, dated incidents from named providers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Specific, dated incidents from named providers are more usable than aggregate complaints."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete examples with dates and identify the ISP involved so the FCC can cite and verify the anecdote. Avoid vague or purely statistical/general complaints without illustrative instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document recurring or systemic problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring issues like "upload throttling customers" and "harassing customers seeking to cancel service" are exactly what the FCC needs to hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem happened more than once or affected multiple people, say so and describe the pattern; name the behavior (e.g., throttling, harassment) and how often/over what period it occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat individual subscriber experiences as proof-of-harm for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: EFF treats individual subscriber experiences as the proof-of-harm record the FCC needs to justify rulemaking — "the agency cannot cite anecdotes it does not have."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame your anecdote to show the concrete harm and regulatory relevance. The advocacy theory is to build the evidentiary base for the rule you want, so tailor anecdotes to illustrate the problem a proposed rule would address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the impacts and link to broader policy outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Such feedback "informs future broadband availability as well as funding, standards, and federal policy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the real-world impact on you (access, cost, ability to use services) and, when possible, connect your experience to how it should influence policy, funding decisions, or technical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete problem examples rather than vague assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete documented problems (e.g., upload throttling; harassment during cancellation) are what the FCC needs to hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give clear, factual descriptions of what happened, including technical effects (e.g., reduced upload speed), the interaction (e.g., customer service harassment), and any attempted remedies or lack thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer first-hand, individual narratives over aggregate complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific, first-hand accounts are more usable to the agency than aggregate or anonymous summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While broader data can be useful, prioritize submitting your own experience so the FCC has anecdotes it can cite; aggregates without specific incidents are less actionable.
